_meta.description: Per-growth-stage environmental sensitivity scores for Pakistan Kharif crops.

action_schema.notes: avoid action_type always has empty adjustment and adjustment_type. sowing and harvesting use only 'delay' as adjustment. Not Feasible entries carry exactly one action with action_type 'avoid'. Ideal entries carry an empty actions array.

soil_adjustment_rules._note: Rice: Clay > Loamy > Sandy | Maize: Loamy > Sandy > Clay | Cotton: Loamy > Sandy > Clay

Clay.reasoning: Clay retains water through natural puddling, maintaining flooded paddy conditions while its high cation exchange capacity supports season-long fertility.

Loamy.reasoning: Loam provides adequate water retention and nutrient cycling for rice with consistent irrigation and field bunding to maintain paddy water levels.

Sandy.reasoning: Sandy soil cannot retain standing water, making flooded paddy conditions impractical and uneconomical even with intensive irrigation.

Loamy.reasoning: Loam's balance of drainage, aeration and moisture retention provides optimal conditions for vigorous maize development.

Sandy.reasoning: Sandy soil drains too rapidly, causing nutrient leaching and moisture stress that reduce maize yield without compensating irrigation and fertiliser inputs.

Clay.reasoning: Clay's poor aeration causes oxygen deficiency in maize roots within 24–48 hours, leading to root rot and growth collapse.

Loamy.reasoning: Loam supports cotton's deep taproot with good drainage and aeration, enabling strong boll development and high fibre quality.

Sandy.reasoning: Sandy soil's low nutrient retention undermines cotton's high fertility demands during boll development without active replenishment.

Clay.reasoning: Clay's chronic saturation promotes Pythium root rot in cotton and causes boll shedding under prolonged wet conditions.

season_adjustment_rules._note: Sowing suitability score per season (0-1). High = good sowing window.

Rainy.reasoning: Monsoon rainfall directly maintains flooded paddy conditions, reducing irrigation demand while warm temperatures and high humidity support all rice growth stages.

Winter.reasoning: Winter cold falls below rice's germination threshold and cannot supply the water availability paddy cultivation requires.

Summer.reasoning: Summer rice achieves high yields with irrigation; warm temperatures drive rapid grain fill and heat-tolerant varieties manage heat stress at flowering.

Fall.reasoning: Declining autumn temperatures and rainfall prevent rice from completing its growing cycle in this season.

Rainy.reasoning: Consistent rainy-season rainfall and warmth support all maize growth stages, delivering strong yields when planting avoids peak-flooding low-lying fields.

Winter.reasoning: Winter cold falls below maize's germination threshold and frost risk prevents seedling establishment in most growing regions.

Summer.reasoning: Summer's high temperatures and long days maximise C4 photosynthesis in maize, delivering peak yield potential with appropriate irrigation.

Fall.reasoning: Cooling autumn temperatures and irregular rainfall cause poor germination and insufficient heat accumulation to complete the maize crop cycle.

Rainy.reasoning: The rainy Kharif season is cotton's natural growing window; warmth and moisture support vigorous establishment and boll development over its long crop duration.

Winter.reasoning: Cotton's frost sensitivity and long growing cycle make winter cultivation infeasible in all but tropical frost-free regions.

Summer.reasoning: Summer heat and high solar radiation drive boll maturation and peak fibre quality, making it cotton's most productive season with supplemental irrigation.

Fall.reasoning: Cotton's long season cannot complete before autumn cold arrives; frost risk during boll maturation devastates yield and fibre quality.

temperature_adjustment_rules._note: Keys: crop -> growth_stage -> temp_band. Rice optimal 20-30C; Maize balanced C4, flowering most sensitive; Cotton thermophilic, needs >25C for germination.

15-20.reasoning: Soil temperatures below 20C prevent rice seed germination; minimum threshold is ~18C and consistent thermal energy is required for uniform crop establishment.

actions.adjustment: daily temperature monitoring; inspect seed-bed for germination failure

20-30.reasoning: Optimal soil warmth for rice sowing ensures rapid, uniform germination and strong early root development.

30-40.reasoning: High temperatures accelerate germination but increase desiccation risk; early morning sowing and increased irrigation maintain adequate soil moisture.

15-20.reasoning: Chilling temperatures slow tillering initiation and leaf area expansion in rice seedlings, substantially reducing biomass accumulation and stand establishment.

actions.adjustment: daily cold damage inspection; check for chilling injury on seedling leaves

20-30.reasoning: Ideal thermal range for rapid rice seedling growth, supporting tillering, root proliferation and efficient nitrogen uptake.

30-40.reasoning: Temperatures above 35C during early seedling stage increase spikelet sterility risk later; increase irrigation frequency to buffer heat stress.

15-20.reasoning: Low temperatures during vegetative growth severely limit tillering and leaf area index development, reducing the photosynthetic base for grain yield.

actions.adjustment: daily chilling injury inspection; check tiller count and leaf discolouration

20-30.reasoning: Optimal temperature range drives maximum tiller production, leaf area expansion and dry matter accumulation in rice.

30-40.reasoning: Heat stress above 33C begins to suppress photosynthesis and accelerates leaf senescence; supplemental irrigation and potassium top-dressing improve heat tolerance.

15-20.reasoning: Cool temperatures at anthesis cause extensive spikelet sterility in rice; pollen germination requires >22C and extended sub-optimal exposure collapses grain set.

actions.adjustment: daily spikelet sterility assessment; document percentage of open spikelets

20-30.reasoning: Optimal temperature window ensures high pollen viability, successful fertilisation and maximum grain set across the panicle.

30-40.reasoning: Temperatures above 35C for even 1 hour at anthesis cause irreversible pollen sterility; flood irrigation and adjusted heading timing are critical mitigations.

15-20.reasoning: Cooler temperatures slow grain ripening and field drying, extending the harvest window but reducing throughput; schedule mechanised harvest during warmest part of day.

20-30.reasoning: Moderate warmth during harvest supports rapid grain drying and easy threshing with minimal chalkiness or breakage.

30-40.reasoning: Excessive heat accelerates grain ageing after maturity and increases chalk formation; harvest promptly at physiological maturity to limit quality losses.

15-20.reasoning: Cool soils below 18C slow maize germination and increase seed rot risk; delay sowing until soil temperature exceeds 18C for uniform stand establishment.

20-30.reasoning: Optimal soil temperature range for maize sowing ensures rapid, uniform germination and vigorous early root growth.

30-40.reasoning: Hot soils can crust and reduce germination uniformity; sow in early morning and irrigate lightly post-sowing to maintain surface moisture.

15-20.reasoning: Cold temperatures cause chilling injury in maize seedlings, reducing root growth and delaying early vigour; additional nitrogen helps compensate.

20-30.reasoning: Optimal range for rapid leaf area expansion, root development and nutrient uptake during early maize growth.

30-40.reasoning: Heat stress above 33C at seedling stage increases transpiration and can stunt early development; increase irrigation to maintain soil moisture.

15-20.reasoning: Sustained cool temperatures during vegetative growth limit internode elongation, leaf area index and dry matter accumulation, permanently reducing yield potential.

actions.adjustment: daily cold damage inspection; check internode elongation and leaf colour

15-20.reasoning: Cool temperatures at tasselling delay silk emergence and disrupt pollen shed timing, causing severe silk-tassel asynchrony and catastrophic yield loss.

actions.adjustment: daily silk-tassel synchrony assessment; document pollen shed timing carefully

20-30.reasoning: Optimal temperature for maize pollination; pollen viability and silk receptivity are maximised, ensuring high kernel set across the cob.

30-40.reasoning: Temperatures above 35C reduce pollen viability by 5-8% per degree; flood-irrigation during tasselling and adjusted planting date are the primary mitigations.

15-20.reasoning: Cool conditions slow kernel dry-down, requiring extended field drying or mechanical drying post-harvest to reach safe storage moisture.

20-30.reasoning: Moderate warmth facilitates uniform kernel dry-down and efficient combine harvesting at optimal moisture content.

30-40.reasoning: Hot dry conditions accelerate field dry-down and ease harvest logistics; cut irrigation to allow rapid desiccation to target moisture.

15-20.reasoning: Cotton requires soil temperature above 18C for germination; below this threshold seeds fail to sprout or succumb to damping-off, making establishment impossible.

actions.adjustment: daily soil temperature monitoring; do not sow until soil exceeds 18°C for 3 consecutive days

20-30.reasoning: Below cotton's optimal 28-32C sowing range, germination is slower and less uniform; delay sowing until conditions warm and apply starter fertiliser to compensate.

30-40.reasoning: Warm soils in the 30-35C range provide optimal cotton germination conditions, ensuring rapid and uniform stand establishment.

actions.adjustment: daily cold damage inspection; check hypocotyl and cotyledon tissue for chilling injury

20-30.reasoning: Adequate but sub-optimal for cotton seedling growth; additional nitrogen and potassium support faster canopy closure under cooler conditions.

30-40.reasoning: Warm temperatures accelerate cotton seedling growth, enabling rapid canopy closure and weed suppression that underpins high yield potential.

15-20.reasoning: Cold temperatures halt square initiation and slow leaf expansion in cotton; biomass accumulation is negligible and boll load cannot be established.

actions.adjustment: daily square initiation check; inspect for stunted growth and leaf curl

20-30.reasoning: Below optimal growth temperature range delays square appearance and reduces the potential boll load; fertiliser applications help compensate for slower biomass accumulation.

30-40.reasoning: Optimal temperature drives rapid vegetative development, early square initiation and strong sympodial branching needed for high boll numbers.

15-20.reasoning: Cotton pollen germination requires >20C; cool temperatures at squaring and flowering cause severe boll shedding and prevent fibre development.

actions.adjustment: daily boll shedding count; document shed squares and apply foliar nutrition to support retention

20-30.reasoning: Below the 30-35C boll-set optimum, cotton retains fewer bolls per plant and boll filling is slower; targeted irrigation and potassium improve retention.

30-40.reasoning: Optimal heat for boll set and filling; maintain soil moisture to support high boll load and prevent heat-induced shedding above 38C.

15-20.reasoning: Cool temperatures slow boll opening and lint drying, increasing the risk of fibre staining and difficult mechanical harvest; allow additional days for boll maturation.

20-30.reasoning: Moderate temperatures with low humidity support clean boll opening, dry lint and efficient mechanical harvesting with minimal fibre loss.

30-40.reasoning: Hot conditions can stress late-opening bolls and raise fibre micronaire; ensure irrigation is fully cut off to promote dry-down and schedule harvest promptly.

humidity_adjustment_rules._note: Keys: crop -> growth_stage -> humidity_band. Rice high-humidity lover; Maize moderate; Cotton dry-climate crop. All crops invert preference at Harvesting (dry = ideal).

<40.reasoning: Very dry air desiccates sown seeds and topsoil before germination; paddy sowing requires humid conditions to maintain surface moisture.

actions.adjustment: monitor seed-bed surface moisture and standing water depth twice daily

40-70.reasoning: Moderate humidity is workable but elevates irrigation demand during establishment; increase irrigation frequency to compensate for higher evaporation.

>70.reasoning: High ambient humidity reduces topsoil evaporation and supports even seed-to-soil contact moisture needed for uniform germination.

<40.reasoning: Dry air at seedling stage accelerates transpiration beyond the young root system's capacity, causing wilting and poor stand establishment.

actions.adjustment: monitor wilting symptoms and topsoil moisture level daily

40-70.reasoning: Moderate humidity increases seedling water demand; supplement irrigation to maintain standing water depth in nursery and transplanted fields.

>70.reasoning: High humidity sustains the moist microclimate required for rapid rice seedling growth and tillering initiation.

<40.reasoning: Persistent low humidity during active tillering drives high evapotranspiration that paddy irrigation cannot fully offset, reducing tiller density and leaf area.

actions.adjustment: monitor tiller water status and paddy water depth twice daily

>70.reasoning: High humidity suppresses excessive transpiration and maintains the saturated root zone rice requires for peak tiller production.

<40.reasoning: Low humidity at anthesis desiccates rice pollen grains within minutes of release, causing near-total spikelet sterility regardless of irrigation management.

actions.adjustment: monitor spikelet moisture and pollen viability; increase canopy humidity by flood irrigation

>70.reasoning: High humidity preserves pollen viability during the brief anthesis window and supports maximum grain set across the panicle.

<40.reasoning: Dry air at harvest reduces field moisture, facilitates rapid grain dry-down and minimises fungal grain diseases during threshing and storage.

40-70.reasoning: Moderate humidity allows field dry-down with acceptable speed; schedule harvest at physiological maturity to avoid weather delays.

>70.reasoning: High humidity at harvest prevents grain dry-down, promotes brown spot and false smut, and leads to high post-harvest losses from mould in stored grain.

actions.adjustment: monitor grain moisture content and fungal symptoms daily; delay harvest until humidity drops below 70%

<40.reasoning: Low humidity at sowing increases topsoil evaporation; irrigate promptly post-sowing to maintain adequate seed-zone moisture for germination.

40-70.reasoning: Moderate humidity provides optimal conditions for uniform maize germination with low disease risk at the seed and radicle.

>70.reasoning: High humidity at sowing promotes seed-bed fungal diseases (Pythium, Fusarium); ensure well-drained seed placement and fungicide seed treatment.

<40.reasoning: Dry air increases seedling water demand; supplemental irrigation at establishment maintains soil moisture above wilting point.

40-70.reasoning: Optimal humidity for early maize growth, balancing moisture availability with disease suppression during the critical stand establishment period.

>70.reasoning: Elevated humidity encourages early blight and damping-off at seedling stage; reduce irrigation frequency and improve field drainage.

<40.reasoning: Low humidity elevates evapotranspiration during rapid vegetative growth; proactive irrigation prevents moisture deficits that limit leaf area expansion.

40-70.reasoning: Moderate humidity balances maize water supply and disease pressure, supporting maximum dry matter accumulation during vegetative growth.

>70.reasoning: High humidity at vegetative stage promotes northern leaf blight and grey leaf spot; avoid overhead irrigation that wets foliage.

<40.reasoning: Dry conditions reduce pollen viability and silk receptivity at silking; critical irrigation during tasselling offsets atmospheric moisture deficit.

40-70.reasoning: Optimal humidity for pollen viability and silk capture; moderate conditions support maximum kernel set across the cob.

>70.reasoning: Very high humidity at silking promotes ear rot pathogens and can clump pollen; ensure adequate plant spacing for air circulation.

<40.reasoning: Dry air at harvest rapidly dries grain to safe storage moisture, reducing post-harvest losses and energy costs for mechanical drying.

40-70.reasoning: Moderate humidity allows timely field dry-down; combine at optimal kernel moisture to achieve quality grain.

>70.reasoning: High humidity prevents grain dry-down, promotes Aspergillus and Fusarium ear molds and renders safe storage impossible without high-energy artificial drying.

actions.adjustment: monitor ear mold development daily; delay harvest and arrange artificial drying equipment

<40.reasoning: Low humidity increases topsoil moisture loss before germination; irrigate immediately post-sowing and apply mulch to conserve seed-zone moisture.

40-70.reasoning: Moderate humidity supports cotton germination with low damping-off risk, providing a balanced environment for uniform stand establishment.

>70.reasoning: High humidity at sowing causes severe damping-off (Rhizoctonia, Pythium) and seed rot that prevent stand establishment.

actions.adjustment: monitor seed-bed disease pressure daily; delay sowing until humidity drops below 65%

<40.reasoning: Dry conditions increase seedling water stress and raise irrigation demand; apply drip irrigation to maintain adequate root-zone moisture.

40-70.reasoning: Optimal humidity for cotton seedling development; supports rapid hypocotyl and tap-root growth without disease pressure.

>70.reasoning: Persistent high humidity at seedling stage causes Pythium seedling blight and bacterial blight, causing unacceptable stand loss.

actions.adjustment: apply preventive fungicide immediately for Pythium and bacterial blight
daily disease scouting; check for damping-off and stand loss

<40.reasoning: Low humidity during vegetative growth elevates water demand; drip irrigation and mulching are essential to prevent moisture stress and boll-load reduction.

40-70.reasoning: Moderate humidity supports healthy square initiation and canopy development with minimal risk of Alternaria or Bacterial Blight.

>70.reasoning: Prolonged high humidity at vegetative stage triggers Alternaria blight and bacterial blight, causing severe defoliation and limiting yield potential.

<40.reasoning: Dry conditions increase boll shedding risk; precision irrigation at boll set stage maintains soil moisture to support retention.

>70.reasoning: High humidity at harvest prevents boll opening, causes severe fibre staining and boll rot, and makes mechanical harvesting highly inefficient.

actions.adjustment: monitor boll opening and fibre staining daily; delay harvest until humidity drops and bolls are fully open

soil_moisture_adjustment_rules._note: Keys: crop -> growth_stage -> moisture_band. Rice: saturation needed except at harvest; Maize/Cotton: 30-60% optimal, invert at harvesting (drier = ideal).

<30.reasoning: Paddy sowing requires saturated soil to establish standing water; below 30% volumetric moisture the field cannot hold the shallow flood needed for germination.

actions.adjustment: check standing water depth and soil saturation twice daily; prioritise full field flooding before sowing

30-60.reasoning: Moderate soil moisture is insufficient for paddy sowing; intensive irrigation must be applied to bring soil to saturation before transplanting or direct seeding.

>60.reasoning: Near-saturated soil enables immediate establishment of standing water, ensuring uniform seed-to-water contact and rapid germination.

<30.reasoning: Rice seedlings require continuous standing water for anaerobic root development; below 30% moisture, aerobic conditions persist and seedlings fail.

actions.adjustment: monitor standing water depth and seedling turgor twice daily

30-60.reasoning: Insufficient moisture for paddy at seedling stage; rapidly increase irrigation to achieve saturation and maintain 3-5cm standing water depth.

>60.reasoning: Saturated root zone supports vigorous tiller production and weed suppression during the critical seedling establishment phase.

actions.adjustment: monitor paddy water depth and tiller condition twice daily; restore continuous flooding immediately

>60.reasoning: Continuous saturation throughout the vegetative phase maximises tiller number, leaf area and biomass accumulation for high grain yield.

actions.adjustment: maintain flood depth at anthesis; inspect spikelet moisture status twice daily

>60.reasoning: Continuous saturation at anthesis protects pollen viability, maximises fertilisation rate and ensures full panicle grain set.

<30.reasoning: Dry soil conditions allow combine harvesters to enter fields safely, facilitating rapid and efficient harvest with minimal grain loss.

30-60.reasoning: Moderately moist but trafficable soil supports mechanised harvest without bogging; cut irrigation 10-14 days before harvest to achieve this state.

>60.reasoning: Saturated soil at harvest makes fields inaccessible to machinery, forces manual harvest and increases post-harvest losses; cease irrigation well before cutting.

<30.reasoning: Dry soil reduces seed-soil contact and slows germination; irrigate pre-planting to bring soil to field capacity before sowing maize.

30-60.reasoning: Field capacity soil moisture provides optimal seed-bed conditions for rapid and uniform maize germination and radicle development.

>60.reasoning: Waterlogged seed-beds cause seed rot and oxygen deprivation before emergence; maize cannot establish under flooded conditions.

<30.reasoning: Low soil moisture at seedling stage approaches permanent wilting point; irrigation must maintain field capacity to prevent stunting.

30-60.reasoning: Optimal aerobic soil moisture for maize root expansion, nutrient uptake and early leaf area development.

>60.reasoning: Waterlogging during early seedling stage deprives roots of oxygen within 24-48 hours, causing root rot and permanent stand loss.

30-60.reasoning: Optimal soil moisture at flowering ensures synchronous pollen shed and silk emergence, maximising kernel set across the cob.

>60.reasoning: Waterlogging at the reproductive stage causes anaerobic root damage at a critical time when water uptake must be sustained; avoid entirely.

ph_adjustment_rules._note: Keys: crop -> growth_stage -> ph_band. Bands: <6.5 (Acidic), 6.5-7.5 (Neutral), >7.5 (Alkaline). Dataset ph is float (range 5.0-8.0). Rice: <6.5 and 6.5-7.5 ideal (flooding buffers acidity); Maize: 6.5-7.5 strictly best; Cotton: 6.5-7.5 and >7.5 ideal.

<6.5.reasoning: Rice germinates well in acidic soils; flooding rapidly moderates extreme acidity toward a near-neutral pH due to anaerobic chemistry, making establishment reliable above pH 4.5.

6.5-7.5.reasoning: Neutral pH at sowing maximises early nutrient availability and supports uniform germination and seedling establishment.

>7.5.reasoning: Alkaline soils reduce iron and zinc solubility, increasing seedling micronutrient deficiency risk; apply chelated iron and zinc at sowing to compensate.

<6.5.reasoning: Acidic flooded soils become progressively more neutral, providing adequate phosphorus and micronutrients for vigorous seedling growth in rice.

6.5-7.5.reasoning: Optimal nutrient availability at neutral pH drives rapid tillering and leaf area development during the seedling phase.

>7.5.reasoning: Alkaline conditions at seedling stage cause iron-deficiency yellowing in rice; foliar iron and zinc sprays correct deficiency without soil amendment.

<6.5.reasoning: Rice's strong adaptation to acidic paddy soils allows high tiller production and dry matter accumulation; nitrogen application compensates for any reduced availability.

6.5-7.5.reasoning: Neutral pH supports peak nutrient uptake efficiency during the most nutrient-demanding vegetative growth phase.

>7.5.reasoning: Prolonged alkalinity during vegetative growth depresses iron, zinc and phosphorus availability, slowing tiller production and dry matter accumulation.

<6.5.reasoning: Acidic paddy conditions support adequate micronutrient supply at anthesis; pollen viability is maintained when other conditions are met.

6.5-7.5.reasoning: Neutral pH ensures full nutrient supply to the panicle during flowering and grain fill, supporting maximum grain set.

>7.5.reasoning: Alkaline conditions at flowering reduce micronutrient availability to developing spikelets; targeted fertilisation is required to protect grain set.

<6.5.reasoning: Soil pH has limited direct effect on grain maturation; acidic soils have supported yield development throughout the season without issue.

6.5-7.5.reasoning: Neutral pH is associated with well-managed paddy soils that deliver consistent yields and quality grain.

>7.5.reasoning: Any nutrient deficiencies accumulated during the season on alkaline soils may reduce grain filling rate and milling quality at harvest.

<6.5.reasoning: Acidic soils inhibit seed germination through aluminium toxicity and reduced phosphorus availability; apply lime before sowing to raise pH toward 6.0.

6.5-7.5.reasoning: Neutral pH (6.0-7.0) maximises early nutrient availability for germination and radicle development, providing an optimal seed-bed chemistry.

>7.5.reasoning: Alkaline soils reduce phosphorus and micronutrient availability at germination; apply starter phosphorus and chelated zinc to compensate.

6.5-7.5.reasoning: Optimal soil chemistry for early maize growth; all macro and micronutrients are fully available, driving vigorous early root and shoot development.

<6.5.reasoning: Nutrient deficiencies from acidic soils at tasselling impair pollen quality and silk development; corrective fertilisation before heading is required.

6.5-7.5.reasoning: Optimal nutrient availability at neutral pH supports full pollen viability, silk receptivity and kernel set during the most yield-critical stage.

>7.5.reasoning: Micronutrient deficiency on alkaline soils at flowering reduces pollen quality and kernel set; apply zinc and boron before tasselling to protect yield.

<6.5.reasoning: Season-long nutrient deficiencies on acidic soils reduce grain fill and test weight; plan corrective liming before the next season.
